Cartesia's Sonic 3.6 takes the #1 spot on both the Provider Voice and Controlled Voice Artificial Analysis Speech Arena leaderboards, surpassing Speechify AI's Simba 3.2 and Alibaba's Qwen-Audio-3.0-TTS-Plus, with Sonic 3.5 holding #2 on Controlled Voice

Sonic 3.6 is the latest TTS model from @cartesia, supporting 40+ languages including English, Hindi, Spanish, French, German and Japanese. In the TTS Arena, the model has been preferred by voters and has demonstrated natural speech and adaptive pacing across conversations.

Key takeaways:

➤ Controlled Voice: Sonic 3.6 takes #1 on the Controlled Voice Arena with an Elo of 1,144 (+18/-18) across 1,339 appearances, ahead of Cartesia's own Sonic 3.5 at 1,099 and ElevenLabs' Eleven v3 at 1,060

➤ Provider Voice: Sonic 3.6 also takes #1 on the Provider Voice Arena with an Elo score of 1,286 (+19/-19) based on 1,300 arena appearances, placing it ahead of Simba 3.2 at 1,238 and Qwen-Audio-3.0-TTS-Plus at 1,237

➤ Pricing: At $49 per 1M characters via the Cartesia platform, Sonic 3.6 is the most expensive of the top three models on quality, roughly 5x Speechify AI's Simba 3.2 at $10 and nearly double Alibaba's Qwen-Audio-3.0-TTS-Plus at $27.59, though still half the price of ElevenLabs' Eleven v3 at $100

➤ Speed: Sonic 3.6 processes 136.1 characters per second of generation time, compared to 46.7 for ElevenLabs' Eleven v3 and 24.2 for Google's Gemini 3.1 Flash TTS

items.title: In 1989 I was jealous of Steve Wozniak for buying a $45,000 color printer so he could print out of P...
items.content:
In 1989 I was jealous of Steve Wozniak for buying a $45,000 color printer so he could print out of Photoshop 1.0.

Today a $70 printer beats it.

But the printer never really got cheap. The expensive part just moved. You stopped paying for the machine and started paying for the ink, and the ink is priced so you never do the math.

I sold consumer electronics for a decade before I wrote about any of this. People will argue for an hour about the sticker price and never ask what's inside it.

AI is at the ink stage now.

Model prices are collapsing in public. What nobody sees is the 5% that gateways take out of every token, priced into the credits before you spend them.

Ben showed me an agent bill running $1.2 million a month. The toll alone on that is $60,000 a month, for forwarding a request.

Somebody just took it to zero.

items.content:
The most dangerous part of an AI agent is not what it thinks. It is what the system lets it do.

Agents have already deleted 200+ emails, wiped a production database, and caused an outage while following what they believed was the correct action.

Another system prompt does not fix that.

Agent security is moving into three system layers:

> Infrastructure: sandbox execution and keep credentials outside the agent
> Runtime: reduce the attack surface and isolate each session
> Network: inspect outbound requests before they leave the boundary

@NVIDIAAI's  NemoClaw handles the infrastructure layer with Docker, Landlock, seccomp, network namespaces, and a gateway that injects API keys only after approval.

NanoClaw reduces the runtime surface with a small codebase and isolated ephemeral containers.

CrabTrap treats the network as the final control point. Low-risk requests pass through static rules. High-risk requests go to an LLM judge and, when needed, a human approver.

The security model changes once you assume the agent will eventually make the wrong decision.

🆕 Context Engineering in 2026: Compaction, Memory & Cost

https://t.co/08qPA63bBd

@Whats_AI, @samridhivaid and @omar_solano1 return!

This workshop is about engineering the context window so rot stops happening, shown with @towards_AI's open-source AI tutor, which answers questions for students of our AI-engineering courses. 

Context engineering is deciding what the model sees on every single call — instructions, history, retrieved course content, memory, and tool outputs — and it's the line between a tutor that holds a coherent session and one that forgets the student's setup halfway through. 

We'll move in three stages, mirroring how the project actually went. The concepts: 

- the two root problems (a finite window, a stateless model), 
- the full compaction toolkit (truncation, trimming, tool-result clearing, summarization, and offloading to files — and when each actually helps), 
- memory that survives across sessions, skills loaded on demand, and 
- production-grade retrieval (chunking, metadata, course scoping, hybrid search, reranking, and evaluating). 

We'll cover the tutor's architecture, and the evaluation harness we used to measure every run on Gemini — tokens, cost, latency, and memory probes instead of vibe-checks. At real volume, even Gemini Flash got expensive, so we tested whether open and local models could match the quality for a fraction of the cost and match result quality. 

Everything is open-source and will be shared during the workshop.

https://t.co/08qPA63bBd

@Whats_AI, @samridhivaid and @omar_solano1 return!

This workshop is about engineering the context window so rot stops happening, shown with @towards_AI's open-source AI tutor, which answers questions for students of our AI-engineering courses.

Context engineering is deciding what the model sees on every single call — instructions, history, retrieved course content, memory, and tool outputs — and it's the line between a tutor that holds a coherent session and one that forgets the student's setup halfway through.

We'll move in three stages, mirroring how the project actually went. The concepts:

  • the two root problems (a finite window, a stateless model),
  • the full compaction toolkit (truncation, trimming, tool-result clearing, summarization, and offloading to files — and when each actually helps),
  • memory that survives across sessions, skills loaded on demand, and
  • production-grade retrieval (chunking, metadata, course scoping, hybrid search, reranking, and evaluating).

We'll cover the tutor's architecture, and the evaluation harness we used to measure every run on Gemini — tokens, cost, latency, and memory probes instead of vibe-checks. At real volume, even Gemini Flash got expensive, so we tested whether open and local models could match the quality for a fraction of the cost and match result quality.

Everything is open-source and will be shared during the workshop.

Don't talk directly to a model.

The simplest trick you can use to improve the architecture of whatever you are building is to introduce a layer between your code and a model.

This will make your app 10x more flexible.

On top of routing, with a gateway you will have:

• fallbacks
• observability
• caching
• cost management
• rate limiting and quotas
• centralized security

Even more important: you will be 100% independent from your model provider, so you can swap models anytime for little to no cost.

items.content:
Here are 22 more gems according to the AI among my bookmarks

1. Researchers compressed 4.1 million recipes into a two-megabyte model of human cooking.

The model spans seven languages and represents 1,790 ingredients in 300 dimensions. Beyond the technical achievement, it suggests a fascinating possibility: representing entire culinary traditions as a navigable mathematical space.

https://t.co/b5Ot6zgquH

2. Scientists watched a single-celled organism evolve multicellularity in real time.

After researchers introduced a predator, a single-cell alga evolved into a multicellular organism. The transition reportedly took about a year—a compressed demonstration of how environmental pressure can produce a major evolutionary transition.

https://t.co/SpZIVNPUbA

3. The human brain contains billions of neurons but appears to process conscious thought at roughly ten bits per second.

This paper asks why our enormous biological machinery produces such a narrow stream of conscious processing—and why we can generally think about only one thing at a time.

https://t.co/E1g7ffUhK7

4. Leaded gasoline may have reduced the cognitive ability of about half the American population.

A study estimated the population-scale impact of childhood lead exposure from automobile exhaust. It is a remarkable example of a mundane technology quietly imposing enormous social costs.

https://t.co/51asPa5sF3

5. Cats may exploit change blindness to sneak up on us.

Change blindness is our failure to notice even dramatic environmental changes while our attention is elsewhere. This post connects the phenomenon to a familiar feline behavior: moving closer whenever you look away.

https://t.co/3WWWa6MkjX

6. When did modern civilization finally surpass the technological achievements of the ancient world?

The answer was far less obvious to people living in 1599 or even 1715 than it seems today. This essay reconstructs how early-modern thinkers assessed their own technology relative to antiquity.

https://t.co/SCwuAZTKnz

7. People in nearly every generation believe that morality is declining.

Even young people often believe that today’s generation is worse than those that came before it. Research on the “illusion of moral decline” suggests that this recurring perception is produced by predictable biases in memory and attention.

https://t.co/FeV5NFLZoM

8. Here is a recreation of an entire GPT architecture inside a spreadsheet.

It is a working nanoGPT with approximately 85,000 parameters, small enough to fit inside a spreadsheet file. Because the data and parameters are visible, it turns an otherwise opaque transformer model into something you can inspect cell by cell.

https://t.co/kKfyNzjvXr

9. Studying the brain’s hardware may not explain human intelligence any more than studying computer hardware explains Excel pivot tables.

This paper argues that human intelligence cannot be understood independently of accumulated culture. Much of what makes an individual capable exists outside the individual—in tools, institutions, norms, and knowledge inherited from other people.

https://t.co/qX1STumeqH

10. When AI became better than humans at Go, human players subsequently became better too.

Professional Go players began learning from strategies discovered by machines, producing an unusual example of superhuman AI expanding rather than simply replacing human capability.

https://t.co/dDHJFDp4iK

11. The familiar integer values assigned to chess pieces are convenient—but not really correct.

A pawn is worth one, a bishop or knight roughly three, and a rook five. But a game as contextual as chess should not yield perfectly tidy integer values. This thread investigates what the pieces are actually worth.

https://t.co/C6uzo3TYTi

12. There is film of Paul McCartney going from almost nothing to the beginnings of a hit song in roughly 45 seconds.

It is a rare chance to watch creative expertise operating in real time: not merely performing or explaining a finished work, but discovering it.

https://t.co/hfcDriBzAI

13. What if The Lord of the Rings had emerged from ancient China?

An artist reimagined Frodo and the Fellowship through the visual language of ancient China. It is not merely a costume swap; it demonstrates how strongly world-building depends on an underlying cultural vocabulary.

https://t.co/p2ZqsFZ3Nn

14. Why does the post-scarcity civilization in Iain M. Banks’s Culture novels remain so compelling?

“Why the Culture Wins” examines the political and philosophical appeal of Banks’s civilization—and why it feels like more than a conventional science-fiction utopia.

https://t.co/kPDFGy2yhA

15. The University of Chicago offers a four-year Great Books discussion course that is open to anyone.

The program provides a structured route through foundational works without requiring enrollment in a degree. Andy Matuschak completed its first year and shared his observations.

This is controversial, but in many cases, humans have become the bottleneck in building software.

You are making everything slower and worse by babysitting agentic coding tools. You aren't better at coding than frontier models, and you are letting your ego get in your own way.

I'm working with @vorfluxai and their platform to build software on autopilot.

"Autopilot" is the key here: their platform is designed to work autonomously, for a long time, with no human intervention.

I like it because they do a lot of the verification I'd have to do myself.

An idea goes in → good software comes out

In my tests, this works well for complex problems and non-trivial tasks.

You don't use this to fix a button's color. You use this to build an entire feature that would take you hours of planning and days of work.

Now, the reason the output is really good is that they have baked in adversarial agents that verify outputs at different levels.

They aren't trying to finish earlier. They are focusing on giving you good software back.

It takes 5 minutes to set up. Connect your repo, give it a task (something big, ambitious), go to sleep, and come back the next day to a solution.

That's it.

By the way, really cool that they built a bunch of ways to notify you when the work is done, and you get a summary video with everything that was done.

Here is the link to their platform: https://t.co/6raqB72VHx

Thanks to the team for partnering with me on this post.

Breaking the Memory Wall: The Impact of Near-Data Processing, GPU, CPU, Storage, and High-Bandwidth Flash on AI Strategy and Policy 

Rationale for Specialization in AI Software by China and South Korea and Outsourcing of Hardware

Why China and South Korea should not manufacture rather Import AI Infrastructure from America 

The AI industry is at a critical point. As hardware logic becomes commoditized, inference economics are shaped more by memflation and the Memory Wall.

Building advanced fabrication and memory infrastructure is a zero-sum challenge. Technologies like High-Bandwidth Flash (HBF) use stacked 3D NAND to achieve ten times the capacity and bandwidth similar to High Bandwidth Memory (HBM). They require significant ongoing capital investment and face major packaging yield challenges.

Instead of investing heavily in duplicating semiconductor fab capacity, regional technology leaders such as China and South Korea could reduce their exposure to fab bottlenecks and supply chain shortages by importing standardized silicon components from U.S. suppliers. These could include GPUs, CPUs, HBM, storage, photonic devices, HBF, and CXL interconnects.

Domestic investment could then be directed toward areas where differentiation increasingly occurs at the system and software levels: abstraction frameworks, dynamic prompt management, key-value caching, and application development. HBF research is a useful example. Flash latency and page-based access cannot be addressed simply by producing better chips, more HBM, or additional storage capacity. They also require changes in how software and hardware are designed to work together.

Being a master at AI software has a different scaling profile from physical infrastructure and can be deployed across markets without reproducing fab capacity in every region. A greater reliance on established U.S. hardware suppliers could therefore leave more domestic capital available for algorithm development, on time release of the AI software, agentic user-interface platform, systems engineering, and TCO optimization.

items.content:
How the layers actually work, in plain terms:

→ 5G Advanced wireless enables connectivity that does not depend on the same buried cable as the wired path
 → Starlink provides a different connectivity path from terrestrial infrastructure
 → Intelligent automatic switching enables failover without waiting for someone to notice

Together they create structural separation rather than duplicated risk. As a @TMobileBusiness Partner, that's the design principle I'd assess first - SuperBroadband is built around two independent paths, not two services that may share physical infrastructure.

The key word is automatic. A backup is far less useful if employees must discover the outage and reconfigure the network while critical systems sit idle.
